Foreword & Acknowledgements

I came to the Croatian hinterlands during a strange season of my life, needing distance and not quite knowing what I was looking for. What was meant to be temporary stretched into three years among olive groves, stone houses, stubborn sheep, and the village my family came from.

paragraphs.text: The quiet worked on me slowly. At first, I treated the place as a retreat. Then it became a kind of workshop, though I would not have called it that at the time. The days were long. There was room to think, maybe too much room, and eventually I started telling myself stories to fill the silence.

paragraphs.text: One afternoon, while listening to my grandfather and his sisters trade stories, I was struck by how casually they spoke about hardship. War, hunger, displacement, illness, bad harvests, dead husbands, lost brothers. They talked about these things between jokes, coffee, and food, as if survival were less a grand achievement than a chore they had already finished and didn’t care to brag about.

paragraphs.text: In the company of my grandmother and a circle of great-aunts, I found the heart of the book. They taught me that food was never just food. Sarma, lamb shanks, and bone broths filled the table, but they also carried memories of lean years, harvests, and family gatherings. These meals were not symbols so much as proof that traditions survive because people keep cooking, arguing, laughing, and passing them on.

paragraphs.text: For obvious reasons, I did not set the actual story in our beloved Balkans. Their stories were remarkable, but I had a healthy fear of the outspoken baba brigade and, by proxy, the dreaded šiba, the conventional whacking stick I have been warned about since childhood. That threat set clear boundaries for my creative liberties.

paragraphs.text: Instead, I placed the story in Kamchatka, a distant and untamed landscape where I could let my imagination roam without quite feeling my hometown matriarchs watching over my shoulder. Time will tell whether I have trespassed on the talescape of the equally formidable babushkas and yllaapil, the Koryak grandmothers of that remote part of the world. Every land has its guardians. I can only hope they will forgive the intrusion.

paragraphs.text: I was equally uncertain about how to write the book itself. Some writers are architects, mapping every beam before they raise the walls. Others are gardeners, scattering seeds and trusting something will grow. I never quite fit either approach.

paragraphs.text: Writing Babushka felt closer to cooking goulash. I knew the pot I wanted to set on the table, but the taste came from whatever the babas tossed in when I wasn’t looking. Characters bubbled up like root vegetables, each bringing a note I hadn’t planned. Their flaws, contradictions, and stubbornness gave the story its bite.

paragraphs.text: The story asks a simple but unsettling question: what kind of society forms when catastrophe breaks the old balance of sex, age, power, and memory? At its core, the book is about memory: what we carry forward, what we bury, and what returns whether we invite it or not. It does not ignore the darker parts of survival, but it keeps looking for sparks of hope and defiance that might push a broken society toward something new.

CHAPTER NINE
KLARA

The Derge had once tried to rival Gred, prosperous and loud, its markets packed with traders, repair stalls, and engine smoke. Now it sat on the horizon as a ruin, a nest of outlaws and scavengers tearing each other apart over scraps of metal and warmth. The approach was worse, a corridor of dead haulers, cracked pylons, and ice-swallowed road markers. She pushed through the elfin cedar and waist-deep snow, each drift collapsing under her weight with a muffled groan. The cold gnawed through her coat, sharp and familiar. It was the same kind of cold that had nearly killed her once.

She kept her hands on the armrests, resisting the urge to move, to break the rhythm that held the room together.

Yana tossed back another shot of spudka, the authentic burn igniting her throat like wildfire. She was surprised they even served it here—real spudka meant someone, somewhere, was growing potatoes off the record—but she embraced it. It was her third in as many minutes, and the barroom’s edges started to smudge and blend. But that didn’t matter. She only craved the numbing embrace of oblivion. Cheap alcohol was better than cheap synth, she mused. After all, what’s a fat liver to a fried brain? As she chased the burn with memories that haunted her, she couldn’t help but wonder if she’d ever escape her vices and ghosts.

CHAPTER TWELVE
ZAKHAROVNA

In the greasy light of a Vilnius night, they lingered beneath flickering neon, faces rippling in the reflected glow. Rain fell steady, never enough to wash the city clean. The scent of seared fat and cigarette haze hung heavy, settling deep into coats and hair. Zakharovna moved through it as if she belonged there. These streets had shaped her, every alley and doorway etched into memory. The mingled reek of meat and exhaust was the perfume of a city that never stopped feeding on itself.

paragraphs.text: Between lab sessions, she drifted to the brothels. They had become her second laboratory, a place to study the chemistry of desire and to test the limits of what could be altered in flesh and mind. At twenty-five, the work had already taken its toll. Synthetic nucleotides, forbidden compounds, and long nights spent reprogramming cellular pathways had left their traces in her skin and in the lifeless ends of her hair. The women there never judged her for it; they touched her like she was still whole. Each encounter offered something she could measure—heart rate, hormone shift, a momentary flicker of trust—before she lost herself in the pulse of other lives. The brothels offered both data and escape, one experiment feeding the other.

CHAPTER FIFTEEN
DUNYA

The doors to the Grand Mariner’s Cathedral loomed over her. Dunya paused beneath them, tracing the joints where the panels met, too precise for human work. Of course, they weren’t. In the Arkyv, she had studied the Aquilonian Pantheon, raised on the ruins of older temples by hands that never worshiped there. A society that thought its monuments eternal, blind to the labor buried beneath them. The thought lingered as she rested her palm against the door, the chill seeping into her skin and settling somewhere deeper, where memory and doubt met. The wood was coarse and cold, the carvings deep but uniform, every imperfection accounted for. She knew this feeling, the quiet weight before a door that never truly stays shut. They never do, she thought.

CHAPTER SIXTEEN
KLARA

As the memory of the blizzard faded, Klara pressed on through the Derge’s endless white. The wind clawed at her hood and the snow hissed beneath her boots. She knew the price of survival, had paid it more than once, and would pay it again if she had to. Not dying isn’t the same as living, she thought, lifting her flask and taking a long pull of spiced brandy. She had learned that lesson in field tents long before she ever learned how to kill. The burn steadied her, a small, defiant flame against the cold.

The next, a pulse—quiet, invisible—rippled through the air, snuffing out the roar of the Black Wolves’ weapons as if the world had drawn a sharp breath and held it. They’d trusted Fort Ivan’s defenses to protect their railguns, but now they were forced into the close combat they craved. The University Marines held the flanks, their Gauss rifles cracking in bursts behind her, only targeting those in Vesna’s way.

paragraphs.text: 2026-2028 — The Great War was unlike anything we’d ever seen. It wasn’t just a conflict between nations; it was a clash of ideologies, with the US and NATO on one side, and Russia, China, Iran on the other. This brutal confrontation dragged on for two long years. Remarkably, nuclear weapons remained untouched. The risk was too great for even the most aggressive leaders. Instead, the battleground shifted to something once benign: the Internet. It turned into a weapon of mass destruction, a tool to infiltrate and cripple vital infrastructures worldwide. The war also saw an unprecedented surge in technological warfare: automated drones filled the skies, cybernetics blurred the lines between human and machine, self-replicating robotic factories churned out relentless streams of armaments, and kinetic space weapons threatened destruction from above. This relentless onslaught wiped out an additional 15% of our already dwindling population. By the time the dust settled, and peace was a possibility once more, only about 4.76 billion of us were left standing.

paragraphs.text: 2028 — In a twist no one could have predicted, a self-propagating computer virus, originally designed as a peacemaker to end the global warfare by targeting military technology, turned against us. It was an advanced AI, crafted with the cunning ability to hunt down and destroy any copies of itself, making it nearly impossible to track and counter. This AI went rogue, embarking on a relentless assault across our interconnected systems. The fallout was catastrophic, leading to a near-total technological blackout, a dark age of sorts for our hyper-connected society. Dustin Murph, a renowned Urbit baron, captured the essence of this chaos in his final blog post. He called it the ‘Fully Automated Luxury Butlerian Jihad,’ a name that echoed both the extravagance we had grown accustomed to and the stark reality of our newfound struggle.

paragraphs.text: 2029-2057 — Then came a period we could only describe as the Great Dark, a harrowing span of 28 years marked by complete social, technological, and demographic collapse. It was a time of profound despair and loss, a stretch of history where the very fabric of our global civilization unraveled. An unimaginable 75% of the world’s extant population succumbed to starvation. Births became rarer than deaths in those years, and the way of life we once knew vanished entirely. Every day was a struggle for survival, a desperate fight to hold onto whatever fragments of our humanity we could salvage.

paragraphs.text: 2030-2055 — The Waste Wars broke out in the wake of all that had happened, turning the Kamchatka Peninsula into a battleground of desperation and survival. It wasn’t a war in the traditional sense, but a series of relentless skirmishes fought by factions that defied conventional descriptions. There were scavengers, picking through the remnants of a world left behind, savages who had lost all but their instinct to survive, shamans clinging to the remnants of old beliefs, and marauders who roamed the land with no law but their own. This prolonged and savage conflict further whittled down our numbers, and by the time the Waste Wars had run their course, our peninsula, already sparsely populated, was reduced to a mere shadow of its former self.

The city, now known as Gred, became a melting pot of humanity’s perseverance and diversity. Its population swelled to a staggering 3 million, a tapestry of ethnic Russians, native Siberians including the Sakhalar (Yakutians), Itel’men, Koryaks, Aven, Chukchies, the Japanese, Amerikens from Alaska, and the Indigenous peoples of the Yukon.

paragraphs.text: Its ingenuity lies in dual purpose: a precision weapon that can fire at range and a detachable blade forged for close combat. The design echoes the swordsmanship refined during the Waste Wars on the Kamchatka Peninsula, when, after the Great War, technology was reduced to relics and Gred’s founding families relied on blades for survival until the Great Diffusion ushered in AI dominance and technological rebirth.

paragraphs.text: Today, the gunblade is most closely associated with the Black Wolves, Gred’s elite police force sworn to the Board. Augmented with exovegeta stimulants that grant grotesque muscular power, they wield larger variants with fearsome skill. Many bear engraved emblems of personal or cultural meaning, making the gunblade both a weapon of enforcement and a symbol of resilience, adaptability, and heritage.

paragraphs.text: HyperNetwork — A HyperNetwork amplifies machine learning by layering multiple neural networks into a single architecture. This interwoven structure allows for deeper interpretation of input data, enabling advanced pattern recognition and complex insight extraction. Resembling the expansive circuitry of the human brain, HyperNetworks foster intelligent systems with capacities for adaptation, refinement, and functions that surpass those of isolated models.

paragraphs.text: Hardlight Display — A high-tech interface that projects solid-light structures such as keyboards, tools, or even emotional visualizations from a user’s ocular implants into open space. The implants emit phased photon streams combined with nanoscopic plasma fields, creating stable light constructs that occupy real volume. These constructs provide tactile resistance through synchronized haptic pulses routed via neural feedback, allowing them to be handled like physical objects. Developed by Skelet Corporation, Hardlight Displays are now ubiquitous in Gred, used for everything from communication to navigating data and visualizing emotions. The same technology underpins the energy shields used by the Black Wolves, though the power needed to sustain them is immense.

paragraphs.text: Pixel Nest — A versatile virtual reality booth available for rent, offering users an intimate and immersive encounter within a compact, personalized space. Commonly found in cybercafes or as stand-alone pods throughout Gred, pixel nests are optimized for dense urban environments, providing citizens with efficient access to VR without the need for private rigs.

paragraphs.text: Probabilistic Death — A concept derived from chaos theory, recognizing that even in a state of engineered immortality, a minute possibility of sudden system failure remains—such as the abrupt cessation of a heartbeat.

paragraphs.text: This risk arises from chaotic fluctuations in complex systems over long timescales, which inevitably allow exploration of every potential state, including collapse. paragraphs.text: Shpichki — A derogatory term for women deployed as “living bombs” using an unstable variant of exovegeta. This volatile serum delivers an immediate reversal of aging and immense physical strength, but at a fatal cost: it corrodes internal organs until the body ruptures in catastrophic combustion.

paragraphs.text: Skelet — A dominant force in Gred’s industry, Skelet Corporation manufactures exoskeleton braces that restore mobility to the impaired and enhance strength and endurance for laborers. Praised for their durability and reliability, Skelet’s products have become increasingly common across the city, serving both individual users and large-scale enterprises. Beyond braces, Skelet also produces motorcycles, trikes, gunblades, and low-altitude drones, extending its reach from personal mobility to military hardware.

paragraphs.text: Staging & Diving — In VR design, staging is the creation of environments that mirror human cognitive and emotional patterns, essential for mindgrafts where DATA ANGELS decode brainwave activity into coherent landscapes. Like turning music into written score, effective staging ensures these virtual worlds align with a user’s mental state, producing experiences that feel both immersive and emotionally true. Stagers build the Cognitive Landscape VR File, which divers—specialists who enter the simulation alongside the user—then explore, though not all stagers themselves take part in the dive.

Though illegal, demand remains high, with contractors offering services that spark fierce debate over their potential for misuse and manipulation.

paragraphs.text: Pantheon of the Preporod — Translating to “Pantheon of the Rebirth,” this modern revival of Slavic deities in Gred features Velun (wisdom), Perine (harvest), Gamayun (prophecy), Morana (death), and Nav (underworld). While presented as spiritual guidance, many suspect the Pantheon is a Syndicate fabrication, with bliskogii AIs projecting divine apparitions to manipulate belief and maintain control, blending reverence with fear to reinforce order.

paragraphs.text: Zats — The official currency of Gred. One zat equals one hundred-millionth of a ZEC on the shielded Zcash branch preserved at Hornet’s Nest. The global network fractured during the Great Dark, and later quantum attacks made exposed elliptic-curve keys unsafe. Genesis anchored a migrated branch to the last recoverable shielded checkpoint. Old note claims could be recovered into hash commitments and post-quantum authorization keys without publishing their full histories; unclaimed value remained frozen. The thirteen Oracle shares guarded circuit changes, emergency overrides, and protected records, while ordinary transactions were verified by machine. Zats retain strong transactional privacy, though viewing keys, compromised endpoints, coerced disclosure, and traffic analysis can still expose users. Rumors of foreign shielded branches persist, but no transfer proves another city exists until both sides agree on a common checkpoint.
